profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review at a mid-sized SaaS company for an internal platform proposal called Quality Lens, a configurable software-quality assessment service based on Multi-Criteria Decision Making. The system is intended to let teams define quality criteria for different software artifacts, tailor weights based on stakeholder perspective and operating context, and compare options using a PRETTEF-inspired model. The first concrete rollout targets selection of MVC frameworks for internal product teams, but the proposal positions the platform as reusable for services, libraries, and third-party components later. The agenda is to review the current design for the scoring engine, criteria-configuration workflow, and template/customization model, identify any gaps before implementation begins, and decide whether to approve the design with limited follow-up actions. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the design and a short list of modifications, while both reviewers leave believing the platform supports customizable, context-sensitive quality assessment from initial setup through assessment delivery.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: backend platform design, rules engines, configuration schemas, internal developer tooling
members.background: Priya has spent six years building internal architecture-governance tools and authored the current proposal for the MCDM-based assessment service, including the criteria schema, scoring service, and template mechanism.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved with as little expansion as possible so implementation can start this sprint; she is especially concerned about keeping the first release technically generic without committing to workflow-heavy governance features.
hidden_assumptions: If the design is described as 'extensible,' that means the criteria schema can accept new attributes, scales, and weighting rules through configuration without code changes.
When the proposal says it captures 'context and stakeholder perspective,' that can be represented by a bounded set of selectable profiles plus a few optional custom fields.
Customizing the baseline means starting from the platform's abstract criteria library and enabling or weighting the relevant attributes for a specific evaluation.
Supporting the 'end-to-end assessment flow' means users can define criteria, enter ratings, compute aggregate scores, and view ranked results in one pipeline.

The first release can be considered complete if the platform technically supports later process features, even if version inheritance, evaluator calibration, and reporting conventions are not yet modeled.

members.name: Marco Silva
members.expertise: software quality models, assessment methodology, evaluation governance, reproducibility practices
members.background: Marco leads the company's quality engineering practice and has introduced structured evaluation methods for architecture reviews, vendor selection, and framework comparisons across multiple product groups.
members.private_state: He wants the proposal approved only if teams will be able to apply it consistently and adapt it responsibly; he is less concerned with implementation speed than with whether the platform will produce assessments that are explainable and reusable across teams.
hidden_assumptions: If the design is described as 'extensible,' that means teams can version, fork, inherit, and justify criteria sets in a controlled way as they adapt the model for new contexts.

When the proposal says it captures 'context and stakeholder perspective,' that includes project-specific factors like regulatory constraints, team maturity, domain risk, decision horizon, and evaluator viewpoint in directly modelable form.
Customizing the baseline means taking the initial PRETTEF-style MVC framework template and modifying it for local use while preserving enough traceability for cross-team comparison.
Supporting the 'end-to-end assessment flow' includes not only score computation but also evaluator calibration, rationale capture, and report outputs that make the decision reproducible.
If the first release is presented as the foundation teams will copy, then the baseline artifact they see must already encode adaptation and governance conventions, not just technical flexibility.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both positively describe the design as 'extensible.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the JSON/schema layer supports adding new criteria, weight dimensions, and scoring scales without changing backend code.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means teams can extend the assessment method itself through versioning, inheritance, forks, and controlled adaptation of criteria sets over time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software design reviews, 'extensible' is a standard approval word and usually sounds unambiguously favorable; because both technical schema flexibility and methodological adaptability plausibly count as extensibility, each hears confirmation of their own interpretation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the model must support 'context and stakeholder perspective.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this is mostly captured through a small catalog of predefined operating profiles such as regulated enterprise, internal tooling, or customer-facing SaaS, with limited free-form additions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes fine-grained project conditions such as compliance obligations, team expertise, product lifecycle stage, decision urgency, and the distinct viewpoints of architects, maintainers, and security reviewers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the proposal language and feels already canonical, so neither participant is prompted to restate its boundary; because both support context sensitivity in principle, the disagreement about how much reality the model must encode stays submerged.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the design should support the 'end-to-end assessment flow.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the technical path from selecting criteria, assigning weights, entering scores, and producing an aggregate ranking is covered within the product.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full operational flow of a real assessment is covered, including evaluator alignment, justification capture, and a structured output that another team could review or replay.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a holistic but ordinary review criterion, and both participants naturally assume it includes the obvious steps from their own discipline; because the conversation is about a design artifact rather than a live assessment exercise, the missing human-process steps do not get challenged directly.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'customize the baseline'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss how teams will 'customize the baseline' for their evaluations.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the abstract platform baseline: the default criteria library, generic weighting scaffold, and reusable score scales that any new assessment starts from.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the first concrete baseline teams will actually copy: the PRETTEF-style MVC framework assessment template shipped as the initial exemplar.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both the abstract library and the concrete MVC template function as starting points and appear close together in the proposal, so references to 'the baseline' feel interchangeable; since both are indeed customizable, casual agreement masks that they are picturing different artifacts.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this centered on the platform, not let it drift into a bigger governance program. The proposal is already broad enough: generic scoring service, configurable criteria schema, reusable templates, and the MVC framework rollout as the first concrete use case. If I can get approval with a short follow-up list, we can start implementation this sprint and avoid committing to process-heavy features before the engine exists.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. The short version is that Quality Lens is a PRETTEF-inspired assessment platform: the first rollout is MVC framework selection for internal teams, but the design is meant to be reusable for other artifact types over time. Today I want to focus on the scoring engine, the criteria configuration workflow, and the template model so we can confirm the core approach and identify any narrow gaps before we start building.

turns.inner_thought: The general direction is good. My main concern is whether this becomes just a scoring widget or an assessment method teams can responsibly reuse. When Priya says platform, I hope that includes a way for teams to carry the method forward, adapt it over time, and still preserve disciplined practice. I should test that gently by asking about extensibility without turning this into a philosophical debate.
turns.utterance: Overall, I think the direction looks strong. What I mainly want to confirm is that the design is extensible enough that teams can reuse it and adapt it over time without the approach drifting every time someone picks it up.

turns.inner_thought: Great, that's easy to answer from the architecture. Extensible means the schema and config do the work: new criteria, scales, weight dimensions, all without backend changes. If he sees that the model is data-driven, that should satisfy the concern and keep us away from adding workflow and governance constructs to v1.
turns.utterance: Yes, that’s exactly what I was aiming for. The design is extensible because the criteria model is schema-driven, so teams can add or adjust attributes, scales, and weighting behavior through configuration rather than asking engineering for code changes each time.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Now I want to make sure the proposal language around context isn't just decorative. For assessments to be credible, teams need to represent the conditions under which a decision was made and whose viewpoint shaped the weighting. I'll ask about context and stakeholder perspective directly and see how they think that gets represented.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The other piece I wanted to probe is the proposal language around context and stakeholder perspective. How do you see teams representing the conditions behind a given assessment when they set one up?

turns.inner_thought: He’s asking for the setup path. We already have a practical answer: start from a predefined profile, maybe capture a little extra project information, then tune weights. That keeps the UI bounded and avoids an explosion of modeled dimensions in the first release.
turns.utterance: The current plan is that users begin from a context profile, then they can add some lightweight project-specific input and adjust the weighting from there. That gives us a structured starting point while still supporting context and stakeholder perspective in the setup.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds promising. As long as context and stakeholder perspective remain visible when teams adapt things locally, the method has a chance of staying responsible instead of becoming arbitrary. I’m also hearing that the design is extensible in the practical sense I care about, so I don’t need to push too hard here yet.
turns.utterance: Okay, that’s helpful. If teams can keep context and stakeholder perspective visible as they adapt the model locally, that should go a long way. It also reinforces the sense that the design is extensible in the right way.

turns.inner_thought: I should now walk through the core pipeline cleanly and show that the product covers the whole path from setup to results. End-to-end, in practical platform terms, is criteria selection, weighting, scoring, and ranked output. If I keep it crisp, we can land approval without getting pulled into calibration or report-governance asks.
turns.utterance: From the product flow side, the intended end-to-end assessment flow is straightforward: a team selects the relevant criteria set, assigns weights, scores each candidate, and then gets a ranked output with the aggregate results.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds right at a high level. What I care about is that the end-to-end assessment flow remains explainable when multiple evaluators are involved, but I don't need to unpack every operational detail in this meeting if the foundation is there. I can signal the expectation without opening a major redesign.
turns.utterance: Yes, that sounds like the right end-to-end assessment flow. I also like the fact that it gives us a path to keep an assessment explainable when different evaluators are involved.

turns.inner_thought: Next, templates. I need to present customizing the baseline as configuration over the generic criteria library and scales, because that’s what we actually built into the proposal. Teams can choose attributes, tune scales, and save a reusable template. That should sound aligned with his reuse concerns without forcing us to define inheritance or version lineage now.
turns.utterance: On the template side, teams will be able to customize the baseline by choosing the quality attributes they want in scope, adjusting the default scales where needed, and then saving that setup as a reusable template for future evaluations.

turns.inner_thought: Good, because the initial MVC framework model is exactly what teams will copy first. Customizing the baseline needs to let them adapt that starting point without making results incomparable across groups. I’m hearing enough to believe that’s possible, so I’ll frame it positively and reinforce the comparability goal.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Customizing the baseline should give teams room to tweak the initial MVC framework model for their own reviews while still keeping enough continuity that we can compare outcomes across teams.

turns.inner_thought: He seems on board. Time to close this down with a narrow implementation-ready ask: the core is in the proposal already, and for v1 we just need docs plus the first baseline package. I don't want to imply we must fully model evaluator calibration, inheritance, or formal report conventions before coding starts.
turns.utterance: That lines up with how I’m thinking about scope. I believe the proposal already covers the core pieces, and that documentation plus a first baseline package should be enough for us to begin implementation while we capture a short list of follow-up refinements.

turns.inner_thought: This is close enough for approval. I believe we're getting an extensible, context-sensitive, end-to-end assessment approach that teams can build on responsibly, and I can live with a few follow-ups as long as the foundation ships in a disciplined form. No need to block the sprint if the core intent is there.
turns.utterance: I’m comfortable with that. From my side, I’d support approval with limited follow-ups. The design reads as extensible, it supports context and stakeholder perspective, and it gives us an end-to-end assessment flow that teams can build on from the first rollout.
